headline: In the presence of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah, an MoU was signed between Bihar and Jharkhand on the sharing of Sone River water
fullText:
Ministry of Home Affairs

In the presence of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah, an MoU was signed between Bihar and Jharkhand on the sharing of Sone River water

This historic agreement has resolved a long-standing water dispute in eastern India

The agreement will provide irrigation water to millions of farmers across vast rural areas of Bihar and Jharkhand, while also ensuring access to drinking water for the people

The agreement reached today is an excellent example of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji’s vision of Team Bharat and cooperative federalism

If all states move forward as Team Bharat, then there is no problem which cannot be resolved

On the initiative of Home Minister Shri Amit Shah, long-pending water disputes between various states that had been unresolved for several decades are being resolved through the Inter-State Council, so far this year, four historic agreements have been reached

Chief Minister of Jharkhand, Shri Hemant Soren, and the Chief Minister of Bihar, Shri Samrat Chaudhary, expressed their gratitude to Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah for the resolution of the Sone River water-sharing issue

31 AUG 2026 6:27PM by PIB Delhi

In the presence of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah, an MoU was signed between Bihar and Jharkhand on the sharing of Sone River water. Chief Minister of Jharkhand Shri Hemant Soren, Chief Minister of Bihar Shri Samrat Choudhary, Union Minister for Jal Shakti Shri C.R. Patil, the Deputy Chief Minister of Bihar, the Union Home Secretary, and senior officials from the Government of India and both states were present on this occasion.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that today’s agreement between Bihar and Jharkhand has resolved a long-awaited water dispute in eastern India. He said that this agreement will provide irrigation water to lakhs of farmers in large rural areas of Bihar and Jharkhand, along with drinking water for the people.

Shri Amit Shah stated that the agreement reached today regarding the sharing of the Sone River's waters is an excellent example of the 'Team Bharat' vision and cooperative federalism championed by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. He said that while all states possess their own distinct identities, if they move forward as 'Team Bharat' within the national context, there is no problem which cannot be resolved. Shri Shah added that this marks the fourth water agreement between states this year, which will enhance water availability for irrigation, rural development, and drinking purposes.

Union Home Minister said that the agreement reached today to resolve the nearly 25-year-old water dispute between Bihar and Jharkhand exemplifies that any problem can be solved through dialogue conducted with the spirit of cooperative federalism. He said that issues concerning vast geographical areas, farmers, rural regions, and drinking water supplies in both states have been permanently resolved today.

Shri Amit Shah said that today's agreement would ensure the availability of adequate water for drinking and irrigation to a large population across the districts of Bhojpur, Buxar, Rohtas, Kaimur, Aurangabad, Arwal, Gaya, and Patna in Bihar. Moreover, water would become available for irrigation and drinking purposes in the Palamu, Garhwa, and other regions of Jharkhand.

Jharkhand Chief Minister Shri Hemant Soren and Bihar Chief Minister Shri Samrat Chaudhary expressed their gratitude to Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah for resolving the issue of Sone River water sharing.

On the initiative of Home Minister Shri Amit Shah, long-pending water disputes between various states that had been unresolved for several decades are being resolved through the Inter-State Council, so far this year, four historic agreements have been reached.

On July 7, 2026, a historic agreement regarding the settlement of outstanding payments was signed among the 'Narmada Award' beneficiary states — Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh — in the presence of the Union Home Minister. This agreement marks a milestone in resolving long-standing disputes among these states concerning cost-sharing for the construction of the Sardar Sarovar Project, with the outstanding dues being resolved through a one-time settlement.

On June 29, 2026, a significant agreement was signed between the governments of Rajasthan and Haryana regarding the construction and implementation of the Yamuna Water Project. Under this agreement, approximately 580 MCM of water will be conveyed from the Yamuna Canal to Rajasthan via three underground pipelines. The project aims to deliver Rajasthan's share of Yamuna water from the Western Yamuna Canal through these underground pipelines. This will enable Rajasthan to effectively utilize the water allocated to it under the 1994 agreement regarding the sharing of usable surface water in the Upper Yamuna Basin. The project will ensure a continuous supply of drinking water to the arid and low-rainfall regions of Rajasthan and foster socio-economic development, thereby benefiting millions of people.

On June 16, 2026, a consensus was reached among the concerned states regarding the long-pending ‘Kishau Multipurpose Dam Project’ during a crucial meeting held in New Delhi under the chairmanship of Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah. During the meeting, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, and Rajasthan agreed to a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for the implementation of the ‘Kishau Multipurpose Project.’ Regarding the project, the Central Government will provide 90% of the funding for the water component as central assistance, while the six states will bear the financial burden of the remaining 10%. An agreement was reached to allocate the water assigned to Himachal Pradesh to Delhi and Rajasthan in exchange for sharing the cost of the project's power component.

headline: Union Minister Shri Rajiv Ranjan Singh, Minister for Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying and Panchayati Raj to launch fisheries Infrastructure projects worth Rs 36.49 Crore
fullText:
Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying

Union Minister Shri Rajiv Ranjan Singh, Minister for Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying and Panchayati Raj to launch fisheries Infrastructure projects worth Rs 36.49 Crore

Major Focus on Strengthening Fisheries Infrastructure to Boost the Fisheries Value Chain and create better livelihoods opportunities

31 AUG 2026 6:08PM by PIB Delhi

The Department of Fisheries, Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying Government of India is organizing a launch of Fisheries Infrastructure Project under PMMSY and Multi-Dimensional Capacity Building Conclave for Co-operative Led Seaweed Farming under Blue Economy on 1st September 2026, at Kamarajar Manimadapam, Puducherry to strengthen fisheries infrastructure, promote sustainable livelihood opportunities for coastal communities, enhance value chain efficiencies and accelerate the development through a cooperative-led approach.

The Outreach Programme will be graced by the august presence of Shri Rajiv Ranjan Singh, Hon’ble Union Minister for Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying and Panchayati Raj; Prof. S. P. Singh Baghel, Hon’ble Minister of State for Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying and Panchayati Raj, Shri K. Kailashnathan, Hon'ble Lieutenant Governor, Puducherry, Thiru N. Rangasamy, Hon'ble Chief Minister, Puducherry, Thiru A. Anbalagan, Hon'ble Speaker, Puducherry Legislative Assembly, Shri Malladi Krishna Rao, Hon'ble Fisheries Minister, Puducherry, Shri G. N. S. Rajasekaran, Hon'ble Agriculture Minister, Puducherry, Shri A. Namassivayam, Hon'ble Home Minister, Puducherry, A. John Kumaradhas, Hon'ble Chief Minister's Adviser, V. P. Sivakolundhu, Hon'ble Civil Supplies Minister, Puducherry, Shri V. Vaithilingam, Hon'ble Member of Parliament (Lok Sabha), Puducherry, Shri S. Selvaganabathy, Hon'ble Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha), Puducherry, Dr. Abhilaksh Likhi, Secretary, Department of Fisheries, Government of India and Dr Sharat Chauhan, Chief Secretary, Government of Puducherry

The event will also witness the participation of fish farmers and fishers including women fish farmers and fishers in person, along with officials from the Department of Fisheries, GoI, Government of Puducherry and representatives from fisheries.

Puducherry is emerging as a model for sustainable and infrastructure-led fisheries development under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY). Blessed with rich marine resources and a vibrant fishing community, the Union Territory has witnessed significant investments in modern fisheries infrastructure, including the upgradation of the Thengaithittu Fishing Harbour and the establishment of a state-of-the-art Fish Landing Centre at Nallavadu. These facilities have enhanced fish handling, berthing, auctioning and safety arrangements, benefiting thousands of fishers and over 600 fishing families in the coastal region. Puducherry is also pioneering cooperative-led seaweed farming through the Advanced Centre for Innovation and Capacity Development (ACICD) at Karaikal, which leverages modern technologies and promotes sustainable livelihoods, particularly for fisherwomen. Together, these initiatives are strengthening the fisheries value chain, generating employment, enhancing incomes and advancing the vision of a prosperous Blue Economy in the Union Territory.

Further strengthening this momentum, the government of India has taken a Cluster approach for strengthening the fisheries value chain notifying Karaikal in Puducherry as a Fishing Harbour Cluster under PMMSY and a Smart and Integrated Fishing Harbour is also being developed in Karaikal with a total outlay of Rs. 119.94 Crore. The modern facility will enable safe vessel berthing, hygienic fish handling and efficient marketing, while improving operational efficiency, strengthening the fisheries value chain and creating better livelihood opportunities for coastal communities.

This integrated approach will support the focused development of Fish Farmer Producer Organisations (FFPOs) and fisheries cooperatives by strengthening their institutional capacity and improving access to modern infrastructure, finance, technology, value addition and markets. By enabling collective action and greater participation across the fisheries value chain, the initiative will help sustainably harness Puducherry’s untapped fisheries potential, enhance incomes and generate new livelihood opportunities for coastal communities.

headline: President of India Graces Combined Convocation Ceremony of NIFT in New Delhi
fullText:
Ministry of Textiles

President of India Graces Combined Convocation Ceremony of NIFT in New Delhi

Students should maintain a Global Outlook while remaining firmly connected to their Roots and the Core Values of our Culture: President Droupadi Murmu

Combined Convocation Ceremony Celebrates Excellence and New Beginnings

31 AUG 2026 6:04PM by PIB Delhi

The National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT), under the Ministry of Textiles, Government of India, marked a significant milestone in the lives of its graduating students with the Combined Convocation 2026 in New Delhi on 31 August 2026. The ceremony brought together graduates from 18 NIFT campuses across the country, turning the occasion into a collective celebration of academic accomplishment, creative endeavours and the journey from learning to professional life.

The ceremony was graced by the Hon’ble President of India, Smt. Droupadi Murmu, Visitor of NIFT, as the Chief Guest. Union Minister of Textiles Shri Giriraj Singh Secretary , Textiles Smt Neelam Shami Rao , DG,NIFT Smt Tanu Kashyap, distinguished dignitaries, members of the Board of Governors, senior officials, faculty members, PhD scholars and graduating students attended the event.

Speaking on the occasion, the President said that the textile and apparel sector is not just a part of our cultural heritage, but it has also been the backbone of the livelihoods of millions of people. If the traditional artisans receive the support and guidance, it will encourage their next generations to remain engaged in this profession with pride and confidence. She was happy to note that various NIFT centres have implemented programmes like the 'Craft Cluster Initiative' to acquaint weavers and artisans in their respective regions with modern techniques in the textile and apparel sector and to connect them with markets. The President said that today, our country is expanding its role on the global stage with far greater confidence than ever before. Fashion Technology is also a field with immense potential to enhance India’s global footprint. She urged graduating students to seize this opportunity. She said that in this endeavour, students should maintain a global outlook while remaining firmly connected to their roots and the core values of our culture. By doing so, they will not only become successful professionals but also contribute to the preservation and enrichment of India’s cultural heritage.

Addressing the gathering Union Minister of Textiles Shri Giriraj Singh urged the students to dream big and work hard to become the integral driving force of Vikasit Bharat. Secretray Textiles Smt Neelam Shami Rao while congratulating the graduating students , asked them to pursue continuous learning and upgrading skills and thus to seize the vast opportunities.

The Convocation recognised the dedication and accomplishments of students who have completed their academic programmes at NIFT. Their time at the institute was shaped by exploration, collaboration and exposure to the changing needs of the fashion and creative industries.

During the Convocation, the Director General, NIFT administered the pledge to the graduating students and symbolically conferred degrees upon the graduating batch. A key highlight of the ceremony was the presentation of 10 Gold Medals to the Best Academic Performers, representing NIFT’s academic programmes across India. Selected on the basis of outstanding academic performance, taking into account their CGPA and semester-wise SGPA, the ten awardees were presented the Gold Medals by the Hon’ble President of India, recognising academic excellence across NIFT.

Following the central Convocation ceremony, campus-wise degree distribution ceremonies were held, providing graduates an opportunity to formally receive their degrees and celebrate the milestone alongside their respective academic communities.

Founded in 1986 under the Ministry of Textiles, Government of India, National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT) is a statutory institute governed by the NIFT Act, 2006. The institute has played a pioneering role in shaping India’s fashion education landscape by creating an interdisciplinary learning environment where design, technology, craftsmanship, research, innovation and industry perspectives converge.

Across its 20 professionally managed campuses, NIFT continues to nurture diverse talent and encourage students to explore new ideas, challenge conventional approaches and develop solutions relevant to a rapidly changing creative economy. Its educational approach combines contemporary learning with an appreciation of India’s rich craft, cultural and design traditions.

For the graduating cohort, the 2026 Convocation represents a passage from preparation to possibility. The knowledge gained, projects undertaken, collaborations forged and challenges overcome during their time at NIFT will serve as building blocks for their careers and creative pursuits.

The graduates now join a growing community of NIFT alumni contributing across fashion, textiles, design, technology, entrepreneurship, communication and allied creative fields. With an understanding of both India’s cultural inheritance and contemporary global trends, they are poised to bring fresh perspectives to the industries and communities they serve.

The Combined Convocation 2026 with 3793 students graduating including Undergraduate, Post Graduate and PhD brought together achievement, aspiration and the promise of what lies ahead. As the graduates’ step into diverse professional and creative spaces, they carry with them the learning, values and experiences that have shaped their time at NIFT. Their journeys ahead will add new dimensions to India’s fashion, design and creative landscape, reflecting the talent and potential of a generation ready to create with purpose, lead with imagination and contribute to the making of a Viksit Bharat.

headline: PM Modi’s Viksit Bharat Vision: India Must Build a Future-Ready Workforce for a Global Automotive Industry
fullText:
Ministry of Heavy Industries

PM Modi’s Viksit Bharat Vision: India Must Build a Future-Ready Workforce for a Global Automotive Industry

Skilling India’s Youth for Jobs of Tomorrow and Opportunities Across the World: H.D. Kumaraswamy

Auto Industry Must Drive the Skilling Push as India Emerges as a Global Automotive Hub: H.D. Kumaraswamy

ASDC’s Next Frontier: Building Skilled Automotive Talent for India and the World

43 Candidates Flagged Off for Romania as India Expands Global Opportunities for Skilled Youth

31 AUG 2026 5:51PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister for Heavy Industries H.D. Kumaraswamy on Monday underlined the need to make skilling, upskilling and employment generation for India’s younger generation a central priority as the country moves towards Viksit Bharat @2047, stressing that India’s skilled workforce must be prepared not only to meet domestic requirements but also the growing needs of industries across the world.

Addressing the Automotive Skills Development Council (ASDC) Annual Conclave 2026 in New Delhi, the Union Minister said India’s automotive sector is entering a new era of transformation, driven by electric mobility, automation, connected technologies, advanced manufacturing and Industry 4.0.

Highlighting the vision of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Kumaraswamy said India is steadily moving beyond being merely a large automotive market and is emerging as a major global centre for automotive manufacturing, technology and mobility solutions.

“India’s ambition should not be limited to meeting our domestic manpower requirements. We must aspire to make India a global source of skilled automotive talent.”

The Minister emphasised that the rapid transformation of the automotive industry would require a workforce capable of adapting to new technologies and evolving workplace requirements. He said the focus must extend beyond simply training candidates to ensuring that young people acquire skills that translate into meaningful employment opportunities.

“Creating greater employment opportunities by skilling and upskilling our younger generation is essential not only for India, but for the entire world.”

He said the growing adoption of electric mobility, automation and advanced automotive technologies is creating new employment opportunities across vehicle manufacturing, battery production, charging infrastructure, servicing and after-sales support. This, he added, makes it imperative to develop technicians, engineers and professionals with specialised and industry-relevant capabilities.

Stronger Industry-Skill Linkage

Kumaraswamy stressed that the responsibility for building this workforce cannot rest with skilling institutions alone. Automobile manufacturers, component manufacturers, dealerships and other industry stakeholders will have a major role to play in defining the skills required for the future and ensuring that training reflects real-world requirements

“Skilling cannot succeed in isolation from the workplace. Industry participation is essential to ensure that training reflects real-world requirements and keeps pace with emerging technologies.”

He called for a stronger and more seamless relationship between education, skills and employment, with curricula, training methods and assessment systems continuously updated in consultation with industry.

The Minister said automobile manufacturers must actively participate in this process and help create a talent pipeline capable of meeting the requirements of an increasingly technology-driven industry.

“We need to build a stronger and more seamless relationship between education, skills and employment. Our skilling ecosystem must evolve alongside the growth and transformation of the automotive industry.”

ASDC’s Role in Building a Global Talent Pool

Kumaraswamy said institutions such as ASDC have an important role in ensuring that India’s workforce remains aligned with the changing requirements of the automotive sector.

He said ASDC must continue to work closely with industry to anticipate future requirements and equip young Indians with skills that are relevant both domestically and internationally.

The Minister said India should look beyond creating a workforce merely for its own requirements and position itself as a global supplier of skilled automotive professionals.

“Our responsibility is not merely to create certified candidates, but to create professionals who can contribute to India’s automotive growth and compete at global standards.”

He also underlined the importance of continuous upskilling and reskilling, particularly as new technologies rapidly change the nature of jobs in the automotive sector.

43 Candidates Flagged Off for Romania

During the programme, Kumaraswamy launched the ASDC Annual Report and flagged off 43 candidates placed in Romania, highlighting the growing international opportunities available to skilled Indian youth.

The Minister said such opportunities demonstrate how India’s investment in skills can create pathways for young Indians to participate in the global workforce.

The ASDC’s work is already expanding significantly. During FY 2025–26, the council impacted 5,08,173 learners, conducted 1,53,240 assessments and generated 2,88,756 apprenticeship contracts across approximately 3,700 establishments.

With the automotive industry undergoing a fundamental technological transformation, Kumaraswamy said the partnership between government, industry, academia and skilling institutions must become stronger.

“India has the ambition, the market and the manufacturing opportunity. Our collective responsibility is to ensure that we also have the skilled workforce capable of delivering on that ambition.”

He said the government would continue to support initiatives that strengthen manufacturing capabilities, promote technology adoption and develop the skills required for the industries of the future.

“A future-ready India requires a future-ready workforce. Through skilling, upskilling and strong industry participation, we can create opportunities for our youth in India and across the world.”

The Union Minister concluded by stressing that India’s demographic strength can become one of its greatest economic assets if the country succeeds in equipping its younger generation with the right skills and connecting those skills to employment opportunities.

headline: Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan attends Silver Jubilee celebrations of Rajagiri School of Engineering and Technology and inaugurates Confluence 3.0
fullText:
Vice President's Secretariat

Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan attends Silver Jubilee celebrations of Rajagiri School of Engineering and Technology and inaugurates Confluence 3.0

Vice President calls for research-driven higher education and stronger industry-academia linkages

Keralam must focus on high-tech industries to create jobs and enable reverse migration: Vice President

“We just cannot produce graduates; we have to understand the demands of the market”: Vice President

“Say No to Drugs”: Vice President urges students to protect their dreams and aspirations

31 AUG 2026 5:49PM by PIB Delhi

Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan today attended the Silver Jubilee celebrations of Rajagiri School of Engineering and Technology (RSET) and inaugurated Confluence 3.0, an Industry-Academia Summit focused on “India, Impact of AI”, in Kochi.

Vice President Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan graced the Silver Jubilee celebrations of Rajagiri School of Engineering and Technology (RSET) and inaugurated Confluence 3.0, an Industry-Academia Summit focused on “India, Impact of AI”, in Kochi today.

Emphasising the changing demands… pic.twitter.com/84ww0GMd1d

— Vice-President of India (@VPIndia) August 31, 2026

Highlighting Keralam’s achievements in literacy, social development and human capital, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said Rajagiri has contributed not only to producing technocrats but also leaders in public life. He congratulated the institution on completing 25 years and appreciated its commitment to combining values with technological excellence.

Recalling the contribution of the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate (CMI) and the legacy of Saint Kuriakose Elias Chavara, he highlighted their pioneering efforts in democratising education, promoting women’s education and adult literacy, and ensuring that poverty and hunger did not become barriers to learning.

Emphasising the changing demands of the technology-driven world, the Vice President said education cannot be limited to degrees. “We just cannot produce graduates; we have to understand the demands of the market,” he said, calling for greater emphasis on research, innovation and problem-solving.

Commending Confluence 3.0, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said stronger industry-academia partnerships are essential to make Bharat a global hub for technology and start-ups. He called for innovative teaching, interdisciplinary research, responsible use of AI and meaningful international collaborations while remaining rooted in Bharat’s values.

Referring to China’s transformation over the past few decades, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said its progress demonstrates the importance of sustained investment in higher education, research and innovation. He urged Keralam to strengthen research-oriented higher education and create an ecosystem that promotes innovation.

Appealing to the Chief Minister, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan said Keralam’s limited land availability and high land costs make large traditional industries challenging, and urged a greater focus on high-tech and knowledge-based industries. headline: Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh Inaugurates first of it’s kind “Green Forge” Complex at ‘National Agri-food & Biomanufacturing Institute’ Mohali; describes it as milestone in genetically modified crop revolution
fullText:
Ministry of Science & Technology

Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh Inaugurates first of it’s kind “Green Forge” Complex at ‘National Agri-food & Biomanufacturing Institute’ Mohali; describes it as milestone in genetically modified crop revolution

“Green Forge” Facility to Enable Controlled Simulation for Cultivation and Experimentation of Genetically Modified Crops: Dr. Jitendra Singh

Advanced Simulation and AI Can Give New Dimension to Agri-Biotechnology Research: Dr. Jitendra Singh

22 Manufacturing Hubs and Eight Specialised Biofoundry Facilities Being Developed to Support Start-ups, SMEs and Researchers

31 AUG 2026 5:12PM by PIB Chandigarh

Union Minister of State (Independent Charge), Ministry of Science and Technology and Ministry of Earth Sciences; Minister of State, PMO, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Department of Atomic Energy and Department of Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh inaugurated first of its kind “Green Forge” Complex at “National Agri-food & Biomanufacturing Institute” (BRIC-NABI) at Mohali. The Minister described this as a milestone in genetically modified crop revolution.

Addressing the National Conclave on BioE3 (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment) at BRIC-National Agri Food Biomanufacturing Institute (BRIC-NABI), Dr. Jitendra Singh said that the newly inaugurated Green Forge facility, with its controlled simulation chambers, will enable the cultivation and experimentation of genetically modified crops under varied environmental conditions, helping researchers assess their suitability for different locations.

Explaining the significance of the facility, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that Green Forge provides simulation chambers in which the quantity and quality of light, humidity and temperature can be varied to create an optimum environment for growing and experimenting with genetically modified crops. He said this capability would help researchers understand how a particular crop performs under different environmental conditions and accordingly assess the locations where it may be suitable for cultivation.

The Minister said that when a new genetically modified variety is developed, an important challenge is to determine where it can be cultivated most effectively. Green Forge can help address this by recreating different environmental conditions in a controlled setting, allowing researchers to study the response of crops before taking them to appropriate cultivation locations.

Dr. Jitendra Singh highlighted the ability of the facility to recreate specific parameters that may otherwise be difficult to reproduce naturally. He noted that the simulation of light quality and quantity, humidity and temperature, and the possibility of integrating advanced technologies including AI, can provide researchers with greater flexibility in conducting experiments. He described Green Forge as a novel facility with particular relevance for serious research in agriculture and medical sciences.

The Minister emphasised that such facilities reflect the growing convergence of biotechnology, advanced simulation and Artificial Intelligence, creating new possibilities for research and experimentation. He said that integrating AI with the capabilities of Green Forge could make research processes significantly easier and open up new avenues for advanced experimentation.

Highlighting the broader transformation in India's biotechnology ecosystem, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that India's bioeconomy has expanded from US$10 billion to US$200 billion, describing the increase as a major quantum jump. He attributed the rapid progress to an enabling approach and greater engagement with the private sector.

The Minister said that the focus of the BioE3 initiative is increasingly shifting towards industry-ready manufacturing, so that research can be translated into products, technologies and solutions. He stressed that scientific work must ultimately be receptive to industry and other stakeholders so that the effort invested in research can generate meaningful outcomes.

Dr. Jitendra Singh highlighted the development of 22 manufacturing hubs to cater to start-ups, SMEs and researchers. He also referred to the National Bio-Foundry Network comprising eight specialised facilities, describing it as an important initiative for bringing together infrastructure for start-ups and entrepreneurs. He noted that more than 50 process innovations are being scaled up, reflecting the growing emphasis on taking research towards application.

The Minister also highlighted work in Carbon Capture and Utilisation (CCU), noting that the Department of Biotechnology is supporting around 38 projects. He said that integrated bio-manufacturing CCU can provide solutions for carbon capture while also addressing emissions from industries such as cement and steel.

Dr. Jitendra Singh referred to emerging areas of biotechnology, including sustainable aviation fuels, the I3 PhD programme and space biotechnology. He highlighted the collaboration with ISRO in life-science experiments, including work relating to myogenesis, cognitive effects and cyanobacteria growth, and noted that India has also made forays into genetics.

The Minister highlighted the work of BRIC-NABI in agri-biotechnology, particularly its integration with bioprocess engineering. He said this work can help convert agricultural waste into nutraceuticals and high-value biomaterials, thereby creating value from agricultural residues.

Dr. Jitendra Singh also called for greater institutional collaboration and clustering, suggesting that institutions located within the same city or region should explore opportunities for closer coordination. He said such clusters could facilitate not only research collaboration but also academic collaboration, including student-to-student interaction and identification of talent across institutions.

Referring to examples of institutional clustering in different locations, the Minister suggested developing a similar ecosystem in Chandigarh, bringing together institutions working in biotechnology, medicine, agriculture, pharmaceuticals and related areas. He said such connectivity could expand the reach of NABI and create opportunities for new ideas and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Dr. Jitendra Singh said that India's biotechnology journey is increasingly characterised by the translation of research into products, technologies and solutions, alongside the emergence of a new model of low-carbon and circular economy. He linked this transformation with the broader objectives of Net Zero 2070 and Atmanirbhar Bharat.

The Minister congratulated the BRIC-NABI team and expressed confidence that the institute would emerge as one of the torchbearers of India's biotechnology revolution, particularly in agri-biotechnology.

Secretary Biotechnology Dr Rajesh Gokhale, Director NABI Dr Pareekh and MD BIRAC Dr Dhananjay Tiwary also spoke on the occasion.

headline: Century-old limit on turning heat into electricity surpassed, enabling ultrasensitive temperature sensing
fullText:
Ministry of Science & Technology

Century-old limit on turning heat into electricity surpassed, enabling ultrasensitive temperature sensing

31 AUG 2026 4:59PM by PIB Delhi

Scientists have stumbled on to a crystalline semiconductor that converts a temperature difference into an electrical voltage nearly a thousand times larger than textbook physics allows.

The thermoelectric voltage generated is so large that it rivals values normally seen only in liquid electrolytes and ionic gels, not in solid, particularly single-crystalline materials.

The discovery overturns a decades-old assumption about the ceiling on this effect in solids and opens a path to a new generation of ultrasensitive temperature sensors, heat detectors, and quantum sensing devices.

When one end of a junction between two dissimilar materials is heated while the other is kept cold, mobile charge carriers drift from the hot side to the cold side, building up a voltage across the junctions. This phenomenon, known as the Seebeck effect, was discovered two centuries ago and underlies technologies ranging from temperature sensors to thermoelectric generators that convert waste heat into electricity.

For decades, the size of this voltage, quantified as the Seebeck coefficient, places an upper bound of only a few millivolts per Kelvin on this effect in a crystalline solid. Most metals generate just tens of microvolts per Kelvin, and even good semiconductors rarely exceed a few hundred microvolts per Kelvin. Only liquid systems, such as ionic gels and electrolytes, in which charged ions rather than electrons carry the heat, have been known to cross into the millivolts-per-Kelvin range.

A group of researchers from the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR), an autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST), along with University of Sydney, Australia, and Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, has now shown that this textbook limit can be shattered in a solid, epitaxial crystal.

The team led by Prof. Bivas Saha along with Renuka Karanje and Dheemahi Rao and colleagues Diksha Dadhich and Sourav Rudra from JNCASR, Ashalatha Indiradevi Kamalasanan Pillai and Dr. Magnus Garbrecht from University of Sydney and Prof. Subroto Mukerjee from IISc, grew thin films of scandium nitride (ScN), a refractory transition-metal nitride, on magnesium oxide substrates using ultrahigh-vacuum magnetron sputtering.

They deliberately doped them with magnesium to compensate the material's naturally occurring free electrons from oxygen dopants. This produced what is known as a heavily doped, highly compensated (HDHC) semiconductor, a material in which positively and negatively charged dopant atoms are scattered randomly throughout the crystal in nearly equal numbers.

X-ray diffraction and atomic-resolution electron microscopy confirmed that the films remained single-crystalline and epitaxial, with dopant atoms distributed uniformly and no secondary phases or precipitates.

In these HDHC ScN films, the team measured a Seebeck coefficient several hundred to over a thousand times larger than the value typically seen in inorganic semiconductors, and nearly a hundred times beyond the earlier known ceiling (exceeding –124.6 millivolts per Kelvin near room temperature, in a roughly 200-nanometre-thick film). This places it firmly above the range previously associated even with liquid electrolytes and ionic conductors such as hydrogels and ionic gelatin.

The researchers describe the result as a solid-state analog of electrolyte-like thermopower inside a fully crystalline semiconductor.

The effect grew even stronger as the HDHC ScN films were made thinner.

“We were not looking for a record-breaking number when we started this work; we were trying to understand how disorder and charge compensation reshape electronic transport in scandium nitride,” said Prof. Bivas Saha, who led the study. “What we found instead is that a fully crystalline, epitaxial, single-phase semiconductor can behave thermoelectrically like a liquid electrolyte. That was genuinely surprising, and it tells us that engineered disorder is a largely untapped route to extreme thermoelectric and sensing performance in solids.”

Fig 1: Schematic of the electronic band diagram of heavily doped, highly compensated ScN exhibiting thermopower exceeding the Boltzmann limit.

The team has built a preliminary prototype photon sensor using an HDHC ScN film with two chromium contacts. Illuminating one contact with a laser created a tiny, localized temperature difference across the device, and the resulting voltage translated to a Seebeck response of –102.4 millivolts per Kelvin, comfortably large enough for classical light detection and, the team suggests, potentially for single-photon-level detection near room temperature with further optimization. Century-old limit on turning heat into electricity surpassed, enabling ultrasensitive temperature sensing

31 AUG 2026 4:59PM by PIB Delhi

Scientists have stumbled on to a crystalline semiconductor that converts a temperature difference into an electrical voltage nearly a thousand times larger than textbook physics allows.

The thermoelectric voltage generated is so large that it rivals values normally seen only in liquid electrolytes and ionic gels, not in solid, particularly single-crystalline materials.

The discovery overturns a decades-old assumption about the ceiling on this effect in solids and opens a path to a new generation of ultrasensitive temperature sensors, heat detectors, and quantum sensing devices.

When one end of a junction between two dissimilar materials is heated while the other is kept cold, mobile charge carriers drift from the hot side to the cold side, building up a voltage across the junctions. This phenomenon, known as the Seebeck effect, was discovered two centuries ago and underlies technologies ranging from temperature sensors to thermoelectric generators that convert waste heat into electricity.

For decades, the size of this voltage, quantified as the Seebeck coefficient, places an upper bound of only a few millivolts per Kelvin on this effect in a crystalline solid. Most metals generate just tens of microvolts per Kelvin, and even good semiconductors rarely exceed a few hundred microvolts per Kelvin. Only liquid systems, such as ionic gels and electrolytes, in which charged ions rather than electrons carry the heat, have been known to cross into the millivolts-per-Kelvin range.

A group of researchers from the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR), an autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST), along with University of Sydney, Australia, and Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, has now shown that this textbook limit can be shattered in a solid, epitaxial crystal.

headline: INS NIPUN COMMISSIONED INTO THE INDIAN NAVY
fullText:
Ministry of Defence

INS NIPUN COMMISSIONED INTO THE INDIAN NAVY

31 AUG 2026 4:43PM by PIB Delhi

The Indian Navy commissioned INS Nipun, the second Diving Support Vessel (DSV) of the Nistar Class, at Naval Dockyard, Mumbai, on 31 Aug 2026, marking a significant enhancement of the Navy’s deep-sea diving, underwater intervention and submarine rescue capabilities.

The commissioning ceremony was presided over by Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of the Naval Staff, in the presence of Vice Admiral Sanjay Vatsayan, Flag Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Western Naval Command. Senior naval officers, representatives from Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL), Visakhapatnam, veterans, distinguished guests and families of the commissioning crew were also in attendance.

Indigenously designed and constructed by Hindustan Shipyard Limited, Visakhapatnam, INS Nipun is a significant addition to the Indian Navy’s specialist underwater capability. Her induction demonstrates India’s growing capability to design and build technologically complex specialist naval platforms and is another significant step towards Aatmanirbharta in defence shipbuilding. It also reflects the contribution of Indian shipyards, domestic industry and associated agencies towards strengthening the Navy’s indigenous capability.

INS Nipun is a purpose-built platform designed primarily for deep-sea diving and underwater operations. The ship is capable of supporting saturation, air and heliox diving and is equipped with remotely operated underwater systems for inspection and intervention. Her specialised diving complex, dynamic positioning capability and associated life-support and medical facilities enable sustained and complex operations at sea.

INS Nipun is also capable of supporting submarine rescue operations, significantly strengthening the Indian Navy’s ability to respond to underwater contingencies. Along with her sister ship INS Nistar, the ship substantially enhances the Navy’s specialist capability in diving, underwater intervention, salvage and submarine rescue.

The ship’s crest and motto embody the spirit of her specialised role and the men who venture into the depths. The motto, ‘Far Beneath, Few Beyond’, reflects the resolve, skill and endurance required to operate in one of the most challenging domains of the maritime environment.

In his address, CNS stated that the induction of INS Nipun reflects the seamless synergy between the Indian Navy, Hindustan Shipyard Limited and the domestic industrial network. He further stated that proving the role-worthiness of all diving systems during sea trials in a single sortie stands as a testament to the nation’s technical confidence and engineering prowess.

CNS emphasised that combat readiness remains the Indian Navy’s highest priority amidst an increasingly contested maritime environment and growing threats to global maritime highways. He noted that, based on the West Coast under the Western Naval Command, INS Nipun will be a powerful addition to the specialised underwater capabilities required to sustain multi-domain operations.

The CNS highlighted that the niche capabilities of INS Nipun, available with only a handful of global navies, enable a swift response to distressed submarines of the Indian Navy as well as partner nations. This capability positions India as the ‘Preferred Submarine Rescue Partner’ in the region, while also providing specialised support for underwater salvage and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) missions.

Addressing the commissioning crew, CNS stated that they inherit not just a sophisticated platform, but also the onerous responsibility to shape the ship’s soul and instil spirit into her steel. Exhorting the crew to live up to the ship’s motto of ‘Nischay, Nirbhay, Nipun’ (Resolve, Fearlessness and Professional Mastery), he urged them to remain anchored in the core naval values of Duty, Honour and Courage.

With the hoisting of the Commissioning Pennant, INS Nipun has formally entered operational service with the Indian Navy, ready to support those who operate beneath the waves and contribute to safeguarding India’s maritime interests.

headline: National Conference on Quantum Biotechnology charts India's path in quantum-enabled life sciences
fullText:
Ministry of Science & Technology

National Conference on Quantum Biotechnology charts India's path in quantum-enabled life sciences

31 AUG 2026 4:41PM by PIB Delhi

India’s quantum science and life sciences communities came together at the National Conference on Quantum Biotechnology with representation from researchers, clinicians, industry leaders, startups, and students, to advance the translation of quantum science into diagnostics, biomedical imaging, drug discovery, and precision medicine, in alignment with India’s National Quantum Mission (NQM).

Prof. Umesh V. Waghmare, Secretary, Department of Science and Technology (DST), highlighted the strategic importance of quantum biotechnology while delivering the keynote address at the inaugural session of the one-day national conference hosted by Qmet Tech recently at the PC Saxena Auditorium on the IIT Bombay campus, Mumbai, Maharashtra. QMet Tech Foundation (Qmet) is the thematic hub (T-hub) for Quantum Sensing & Metrology set up under NQM at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay campus, with support from DST.

Quantum biotechnology sits at the intersection of quantum sensing, imaging, and computing with the life sciences - an emerging frontier where quantum-grade measurement is beginning to unlock biological questions that conventional instrumentation cannot reach. The conference was designed as an interdisciplinary platform to define national research directions in this space and to strengthen the pathway from laboratory demonstration to deployable healthcare technology.

“Unless we work on all sides of the technology in an integrated and strategic manner, we cannot take India ahead in the technology domain,” Prof. Shireesh Kedare, Director, IIT Bombay said, highlighting the institute’s role in convening interdisciplinary national platforms.

"Quantum biotechnology is where our sensing capabilities meet real clinical needs. At Qmet Tech, we are building quantum sensors of remarkable precision. The task now is to point them at the questions biology has been unable to answer. Bringing physicists, biologists, and industry into one room is how that translation begins," underlined Prof. Kasturi Saha, Project Director, Qmet Tech Foundation, on Qmet Tech’s quantum sensing capabilities and their application to biosensing.

"What struck me today is how much industry interest quantum biotechnology is attracting. Qmet Tech's role is to convert it into deployable technology, supporting startups, developing talent, and creating the manufacturing and testing capability India will need as these tools move towards the clinic, " said Hardik Joshi, CEO Qmet Tech Foundation.

The programme was structured around three sessions. These were on quantum for biology and the academic landscape, translating quantum biosensors--from lab to industry and innovating for applications in biosensing. A panel discussion was held on ‘Quantum Biotechnology in India: Opportunities, Challenges, and the Path Forward’.

Dr. JBV Reddy, Head, Quantum Technology Cell, DST, Dr. Rajneesh Gaur, Scientist ‘F’, Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Prof. Himadri Dhar, IIT Bombay, as well as Prof. Swaroop Ganguly, IIT Bombay, Mr. Hardik Joshi, CEO, Qmet Tech Foundation participated in the deliberations.

By bringing quantum sensing, imaging, computing, and biotechnology into a single forum, the National Conference on Quantum Biotechnology reinforced the National Quantum Mission’s objective of building a collaborative, application-driven quantum ecosystem and positioning quantum-enabled life sciences as a priority frontier for India’s research and healthcare innovation agenda.

headline: NPCI International and Uzbekistan’s NIPC Partner to Enable UPI Payments Across Uzbekistan via UZQR
fullText:
Ministry of Finance

NPCI International and Uzbekistan’s NIPC Partner to Enable UPI Payments Across Uzbekistan via UZQR

Indian tourists, business travellers and students can make instant merchant payments by scanning Uzbekistan’s national interoperable QR code, UZQR

Partnership between NIPL and Uzbekistan’s National payment system marks a significant step in expanding UPI’s international footprint

31 AUG 2026 4:14PM by PIB Delhi

NPCI International Payments Ltd. (NIPL), the international arm of the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), has entered into a commercial agreement with the National Interbank Processing Centre JSC (NIPC), operator of Uzbekistan’s national payment system, HUMO, on 30th August 2026. The partnership enables Indian travellers to scan Uzbekistan’s national interoperable QR code UZQR using their familiar UPI-enabled applications to make instant merchant payments across the country.

The announcement was made during the bilateral visit of the Prime Minister of India to Uzbekistan. The execution of the agreement follows formal approvals from financial regulators, including the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Central Bank of Uzbekistan (CBU), which designated HUMO as NIPL’s authorised partner for cross-border merchant acceptance.

Key Highlights of the Agreement

Universal Merchant Acceptance: By integrating with CBU’s mandated Unified National QR infrastructure (UZQR), UPI users gain near-universal acceptance across retail, hospitality, and service merchants in Uzbekistan.

Seamless Travel Experience: Indian tourists, business travellers, and students can make direct person-to-merchant (P2M) payments from their Indian bank accounts, eliminating foreign exchange markup friction and reducing reliance on international cards or cash.

Strengthened Bilateral Ties: The initiative advances digital public infrastructure cooperation and aligns with both nations' broader strategic and economic goals.

UPI is Accepted in Ten Countries

Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and Greece, enabling Indian travellers to make seamless payments abroad through UPI.

headline: Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw addressed media on Semicon 2.0
fullText:
Ministry of Electronics & IT

Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw addressed media on Semicon 2.0

Notifications for all 6 Pillars of Semicon 2.0 issued

India achieved target of developing 85,000 semiconductor engineers in four years against 10-year target: Ashwini Vaishnaw

Close to 10% of the global semiconductor industry’s market will be in India in the coming years: Ashwini Vaishnaw

Students from Tier-II and Tier-III cities have designed more than 250 semiconductor chips: Ashwini Vaishnaw

31 AUG 2026 4:12PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology, Railways and Information & Broadcasting, Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw, today addressed the media and outlined the Government’s vision for taking India’s semiconductor ecosystem to the next level. On the occasion, notifications for all six pillars of the Semicon 2.0 Scheme were issued, marking a significant step towards strengthening India’s semiconductor design and manufacturing capabilities.

The scheme builds on the momentum generated by the first Semicon India Programme and provides fiscal and infrastructure support across the semiconductor value chain from chip design, fabrication and packaging to equipment, materials, research and development, and talent development.

The scheme aims to strengthen India’s economic growth and national security by improving semiconductor supply-chain resilience and establishing technological leadership in critical sectors. It will operate through six pillars covering 10 categories.

The six pillars under Semicon 2.0 are:

• Pillar 1 - Design

• Pillar 2 - Machines and Materials

• Pillar 3 - Setting up more Fabs

• Pillar 4 - Further strengthening the ATMP/OSAT industry

• Pillar 5 - Research and Development

• Pillar 6 - Talent Development

Pillar 1 - Design: Categories: Design of Semiconductor IPs, Chips, System-on-Chips (SoCs), and Modules for National Importance and Strategic Priorities; Design of Semiconductor IPs, Chips and SoCs for the Commercial Sector; and Deployment-Linked Incentive (DLI) for Semiconductor IPs/Chips/SoCs for deployment.

Pillar 2 - Machines and Materials: Category: Semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.

Pillar 3 - Setting up more Fabs: Categories: Silicon Semiconductor Wafer Fabs; Compound Semiconductors/Photonics/Sensors (including MEMS) Fab/Discrete Semiconductors Fab; and Display Fabs.

Pillar 4 - Further strengthening the ATMP/OSAT industry: Category: Semiconductor Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging (ATMP) / Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) Facility.

Pillar 5 - Research and Development: Category: R&D for advanced semiconductor technologies.

Pillar 6 - Talent Development: Category: Talent Development.

During the event Shri Ashwini Vaishnaw said “India achieved its target of developing 85,000 semiconductor engineers over a period of 10 years in just four years, and has now set a new target of developing one lakh more engineers. In the coming years, close to 10% of the global semiconductor industry’s market is expected to be in India. Students from Tier-II and Tier-III cities have already designed more than 250 chips. In one case, commercial production commenced within just 13 months of the groundbreaking, while approvals were granted within 200 days, 150 days and even 90 days in multiple cases. The semiconductor ecosystem being developed in India is also expected to create 50,000–60,000 direct jobs.”

Projects supported under Semicon 2.0 will generally have a duration of up to six years, while the scheme will initially remain open for applications for three years.

The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) will be the nodal agency for Semicon 2.0. It will invite applications, undertake technical and financial appraisal, recommend applicants and oversee implementation. ISM may implement the design and deployment categories with the assistance of C-DAC. The mission may also announce semiconductor deep-tech awards from 2026 to promote niche innovation.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology will make budgetary provisions for fiscal support, with disbursements undertaken by the nodal agency in accordance with approved conditions. A mid-term assessment will be conducted after three years of implementation, or as required, to evaluate the scheme’s impact and consider modifications or continuation.
